Link prediction is crucial for accurately modeling network evolution, particularly in scenarios where data is sparse. Although Simplicial Sets (SSets) have proven effective at capturing various structural motifs and topological features in networks, their resource-intensive nature makes them unsuitable for very large, sparse networks. To address this limitation, we introduce Sparse SSet Networks (SSNet), a streamlined approach for creating SSet-based node representations. By streamlining the process of constructing SSet neighborhoods, SSNet achieves high efficiency without sacrificing predictive performance. Extensive experiments across diverse link prediction and network classification tasks confirm that our method yields state-of-the-art outcomes.

The rapid advancement of quantum technologies has created a significant demand for a scalable solution to the photon absorption challenge. One potential solution involves silicon atomic vapor chambers, which offer strong light transmission and the ability to interface quantum photons directly with trappable atomic spins using spin-photon interfaces. Nevertheless, prior silicon chambers suffered from compromised light transmission due to limitations in fabrication methods. In this study, we present a solution featuring micro-fabricated silicon chambers with significantly enhanced transmission. This achievement is attributed to deep etching and the integration of micro-optical components. The deep etching minimizes light absorption by reducing chamber dimensions, while micro-optical elements optimize transmission through proper light coupling and minimization of reflection. This work demonstrates micro-fabricated silicon chambers with superior transmission characteristics, establishing them as a vital component for future quantum networks.

Wildfires are a critical and expanding threat to life and the environment, particularly as climate change expands their geographic scope. While visible light cameras are standard for detecting active fires, they often fail during heavy rain or fog and struggle to capture the heat radiation characteristic of hot objects in all weather. In contrast, infrared (IR) cameras can identify fires regardless of weather or visibility conditions. This study introduces FIRe-GAN, a novel deep learning-based fusion framework designed to generate realistic fire imagery resembling visible light despite actual infrared detection. FIRe-GAN specifically capitalizes on the inherent contrast found in glowing infrared fire sources. Experimental results demonstrate that the generated images replicate spatial contrast patterns and color gradients typical of visible light fire images, establishing that the model successfully fuses infrared data into realistic visuals without actual ambient visible light. This represents a distinct advancement over existing synthetic fusion methods.

The successful operation of quantum computers relies heavily on specialized hardware capable of providing an extremely cold, isolated, and vibration-free environment. A new ultra-low temperature (ULTE) platform has been created at Fermilab to satisfy these requirements, utilizing a pulsed adiabatic demagnetization refrigerator combined with multiple heat exchangers and thermal isolation techniques. This system delivers stability below 100 millikelvin at the target quantum computing node for over 24 hours, displaying no detectable vibrations or heat interference. A key feature is its integrated active vibration cancellation subsystem, which uses external accelerometers and a loudspeaker with a microphone to project anti-phase vibrations and nullify acoustic noise. Real-time feedback adjusts the cancellation vibrations dynamically, achieving vibration levels approximately ten times beneath the threshold of detection. This pioneering millikelvin infrastructure offers a robust foundation for large-scale quantum computing investigations.

Detecting the low-energy recoils of a target nucleus is essential for using gas time projection chambers as gas-based detectors, particularly when aiming to observe nuclear recoil signatures from a $^{129}\text{Xe}$ target. This study aims to identify observables that can clearly isolate nuclear recoil events caused by WIMPs interacting with $^{129}\text{Xe}$. A primary challenge in analyzing large-scale datasets, such as those used for vehicle safety assessment, stems from the scarcity of context-rich information regarding incidents like accidents or near-misses. While automated systems have traditionally evaluated commercial driving by ranking vehicles based on the frequency of such events, they frequently overlook critical context, resulting in biased evaluations that harm drivers. We introduce "SECRIS," a novel framework designed to produce fairer vehicle evaluations by integrating driver context with near-miss identification. SECRIS employs machine learning to automatically identify incidents within video footage and utilizes driver experts to contextualize these incidents. This human-in-the-loop workflow enables the training of contextual video models that factor expert input into their assessments. Our approach significantly outperforms non-contextual models in both accuracy and fairness metrics.

Since the beginning of 2022, the GPT-3 Challenge has been running to test the limits of large language models (LLMs) in specific, difficult scenarios. While LLMs have shown remarkable success in various natural language processing subfields, they frequently fail at tasks that require a deep understanding of a domain's context. To address this, the challenge introduces a new format: requiring models to provide answers based solely on a short prompt, without any background knowledge outside that prompt. Participants are tasked with creating specific sub-tasks that strictly adhere to this constraint, along with providing human-verified ground-truth data for those tasks to ensure fairness. This paper outlines the design of the sub-tasks, presents participant leaderboards, and evaluates the best-performing submissions for each.

This study examines a collection of coupled stochastic differential equations (SDEs) within the framework of a manifold structure. To achieve a geometrically rigorous description, we utilize the probability field to define a specific metric, creating a field of geodesics where each probabilistic path is represented by a HJD function. Consequently, field curvature emerges as the HJD function's curvature. To facilitate practical application, we approximate the probability field using a finite-dimensional expansion of HJD functions, which yields an approximation of the metric. Leveraging this metric, we compute the associated geodesics to represent the evolution of the probability distribution. We validate this theoretical framework by applying it to a population of SDE-driven oscillators and a network of Kuramoto phase units.

The shift toward contact reduction and remote activities caused by the pandemic has intensified urban isolation. This study integrates GPS data, mobile phone records, and survey information to investigate changes in movement and social patterns across three major Chinese cities from 2015 to 2020. While the intercity differences in interaction patterns remained largely consistent throughout this period, both the 2015–2020 span and the comparison with 2020 reveal trends toward lower frequency, broader geographical spread, and more dispersed activity types. Specifically, 2020 interactions involved 10% more activity categories on average than those in 2015 and 2017 combined. Furthermore, while 2015 showed a strong correlation between city-level income and interaction density, this correlation disappeared in 2020, indicating that urban sprawl now serves as a significant factor influencing social connectivity independent of economic status.

This study evaluates two nonlinear field-split preconditioners for the nonlinear equation solver in porous media two-phase flow problems. A nonlinear switch mechanism directs the application of either the nonlinear field-split preconditioner by Olee$^r$, or an alternative variant proposed in this research. The two approaches are fundamentally similar except for discrepancies in how field projections are applied. Olee$^r$'s preconditioner applies the split in field space using modal decomposition projections, whereas this research presents an equivalent preconditioner utilizing permutation-based field exchange. Ongoing research suggests the modal decomposition approach may be less efficient for two-phase systems, prompting the need for a detailed numerical comparison. This paper presents such a comparison, specifically focusing on the impact of these precondition strategies on two-phase simulations across various heterogeneous, porous structures.

This study presents an asymmetric optical cavity design that permits light to enter solely through one terminal, effectively blocking entry from the terminal at the output end. By utilizing spatially varying dispersion, the cavity supports modes featuring distinct eigenvalues for forward and backward light propagation in addition to enabling one-way transmission. These findings offer a pathway for compact, chiral optical components and provide a foundation for exploring unique phenomena such as the absence of backscattering and the formation of edge states.

We introduce a technique to investigate the performance of ion traps by measuring spin dephasing rates in a two-dimensional ion crystal. Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) represents a highly sensitive technique that merges the spatial resolution capabilities of scanning probe microscopy with those of Raman spectroscopy. Ultimately, we examined the influence of tip geometry, the distance separating the tip and the surface, plasmonic resonances, and the local chemical environment on both the electromagnetic and chemical enhancement factors.

Visualizing multivariate time series represents a significant challenge because datasets containing numerous time-ordered variables often surpass human cognitive capacity. While current tools for multivariate time series interaction rely on visual encodings that are sparse, these approaches fail to fully leverage the rich contextual details available from such data. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel framework for interacting with both individual and collections of screens, capable of conveying both temporal and longitudinal data through its unique interface. Digital Health Record (DHR) systems have become essential for managing patient care, yet their vast scale and heterogeneous data types hinder efficient querying. While current search engines often rely on the simplicity of exact or fuzzy matches, they fail to capture the complex multi-relational structures within DHR data. To address this, we propose the Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network (DSGNN), a method designed to conduct effective searches across both natural language and tabular DHR data. DSGNN constructs a knowledge graph for each patient and simultaneously learns embedding vectors for all entities to predict similarity scores against a new query. Significantly, the model is capable of generating multiple similar yet distinct answers and ranking these diverse candidates. In production environments, Neural Machine Translation (NMT) faces significant memory limitations, often restricting the maximum context length to 512 states. In contrast, production systems frequently encounter contexts exceeding 1,000 tokens, which standard NMT architectures cannot handle effectively due to these memory bottlenecks. To address this, we introduce a new approach that expands the extractive context length by utilizing a forward-and-backward attention mechanism. This process involves two phases: first, generating an initial translation with original extractive context encoding; second, creating a condensed version of the original context using the translation as an anchor point to apply extractive attention, thereby generating a new context state. Finally, the model combines both the initial and translated context states to produce the final output. Experimental results demonstrate that increasing the memory state capacity allows for processing context lengths of 1,024 tokens without compromising translation quality.

We introduce a statistical analysis of gamma-ray emission from galaxy clusters, based on a sample of 14 sources detected by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT) with confirmed associations. Our findings indicate that, across the majority of cluster sources, corrected fluxes remain statistically indistinguishable from one another. This result strongly favors a non-thermal origin for the gamma rays, likely arising from the magnetic fields within the intercluster medium. Additionally, we explore potential non-gravitational contributions from AGN, estimating an average AGN luminosity of $10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$ in the context of these observations.

Elucidating the internal mechanisms of a Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN) is vital for better training and more reliable predictions. HVFA operates through two sequential stages: initially, it filters out unimportant information by evaluating the significance of each filter across class scores. Subsequently, it visualizes the remaining relevant filters and refines them to highlight high-scoring regions. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that not only does HVFA enhance existing visualization methods in both interpretability and clarity, but it also substantially boosts DCNN performance—improving classification accuracy by 1.5% on ImageNet and yielding 10% higher consistency in annotated classes.

Fermionic quasiparticles serve as the cornerstone for describing low-temperature phenomena in most condensed matter systems. The performance achieved by large language models, such as GPT-3, has prompted a significant surge in human language generation tasks. This surge has created an urgent demand for efficient systems capable of locating qualified workers on platforms like Mechanical Turk (mTurk), which are essential for creating high-quality human-earned evaluation datasets and fine-tuning corpora. Although existing research has explored worker identification and retention strategies to enhance efficiency, it has not sufficiently addressed the specific challenges inherent in summarization tasks. Consequently, this study introduces a novel framework for matching appropriate humans with summarization- focused microtask assignments. By analyzing the performance trajectories of individual contributors over time, this approach aims to streamline the selection of reliable human annotators across extensive mTurk datasets.

Text-video retrieval (TVR) involves matching user queries with relevant clips from vast video collections. However, the diverse characteristics of both textual and visual data make this task difficult. This difficulty is intensified when dealing with short-tail queries, which involve infrequent or rare terms that tend to yield poor semantic representations. This paper introduces Token Shift-Selection Network (TSN) to address this issue. Its primary goal is to facilitate the effective association of text and visual features. Specifically, TSN employs a dual mechanism: (1) **Token Shift**: It aligns token-level text embeddings with frame-level video representations to enhance local feature consistency; **(Choice)**: It utilizes a choice module to integrate token-level signals with frame-level context, thereby capturing high-level semantic alignments. Additionally, TSN is designed to leverage complementary information across multiple input modalities. Experimental evaluations on two large-scale retrieval benchmarks demonstrate that the method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches, with gains of up to **7.3%** on Query2Answer and **5.3%** on QueryStarts datasets. Furthermore, the code and models are publicly available at **https://github.com/THUAI2/TS2**.

Through a comprehensive study of exact numerical simulations and analytical derivations, we investigate the impact of spin-orbit coupling in correlated bosonic systems subjected to a periodic potential. We demonstrate that optical superlattices can effectively switch the modulated superfluid between gapped and gapless regimes. Specifically, our exact numerical simulations of the $n$-th order Binder cumulant reveal that the transition between these two fluid states can be either first-order or continuous second-order, contingent upon the lattice type and whether the system resides below or above the critical temperature. Furthermore, we derive an analytical expression for the Binder cumulant in the non-interacting regime near the Fermi energy, successfully capturing spin-orbit-induced shifts in both gapped and gapless order parameters across diverse temperatures.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, and denote by $G^{\#}$ the set $G$ excluding its identity element. A graph with vertex set $V(G)$ is defined as group-based if this vertex set forms a group; specifically, it is a subgroup-based graph if $V(G)$ constitutes a proper subgroup of a larger group structure. In this work, we investigate a graph where two distinct elements $x$ and $y$ are adjacent precisely when their product $xy^{-1}$ lies within a specified subset $S \subseteq G^{\#}$, referred to as $G(S)$. Although initial investigations into $G(S)$ have been scarce for instances where $|G| > 60$, our primary objective here is to analyze the connectivity of these graphs. We present sufficient conditions for connectivity that hold regardless of the order of $G$, yet remain effective regardless of the specific subset $S$ chosen. Additionally, we examine fundamental structural attributes of $G(S)$, including regularity, isomorphism classes, and the existence of an overarching classification for the graphs generated by cyclic and abelian groups of order 60.

Gaussian process (GP) regression has become a highly utilized tool in various fields, particularly for addressing noisy data. Key to its effectiveness is the selection of an appropriate kernel function (covariance), which dictates how the model behaves. Traditionally, kernel development has relied on a two-step process: first, deriving a physical relationship for the quantity being observed, and second, converting this relationship into a mathematical expression to serve as the kernel. However, this fundamental approach has two significant limitations. First, the resulting kernel often fails to align with the data because the underlying physics describes the true target only approximately. Second, deriving explicit functional relationships for empirical data sets is often unfeasible. This study introduces a streamlined methodology for deriving kernels directly from fundamental mathematical expressions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through applications in regression and time series forecasting.

Accurate determination of the inter-beat interval (IBI) is vital for health monitoring, particularly in clinical settings, as signal quality in healthcare contexts often suffers from noise and degradation. Consequently, developing a system that can reliably and accurately extract IBI from low-quality electrocardiogram (ECG) and pulse signals is essential. This paper introduces a novel signal processing strategy that combines deep learning with advanced pre-processing techniques. While deep learning offers the advantage of automating feature extraction, the proposed method enhances Tiramisu—a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network—through a specialized pre-processing pipeline. This framework identifies heartbeat locations (onsets) by integrating both time-domain and frequency-domain characteristics. Experimental results indicate an overall identification success rate of 98.8%, achieving a mean Inter-Onset Beat Interval (IOBI) accuracy of 67.8 ms, with less than a 1% error related to quarter beats per minute (BPM). Additionally, the system maintains an onsets detection performance characterized by a Positive Predicted Value (PPV) of 98.8%, Sensitivity of 98.8%, and Error Score of 1.88%.

We introduce a novel representation learning method that reframes the learning process as discovering an optimal structure within the Discrete Sinkhorn Vertex (m-Sink) graph. This graph represents a metric space and is constructed by iteratively computing Sinkhorn distances; each distance calculation iteratively refines embedding quality by transforming a uniform distribution into one that mirrors the desired target structure. To enhance these representations, we introduce a deep multi-Sinkhorn autoencoder capable of learning manifold-based distributions for matrix inputs, facilitating robust matrix factorization and dimensionality reduction. We further extend this approach for matrix-based deep learning by developing a multi-Sinkhorn autoencoder that learns from these manifold distributions. Experimental results indicate that this deep framework surpasses both deep metric learning and deep factorization baselines in various tasks, including matrix factorization, image retrieval, and visual relationship detection. Additionally, we demonstrate that this multi-Sinkhorn autoencoder effectively learns from both matrix inputs and pixel-based images, successfully executing image retrieval and visual relationship detection.

Dividing a graph into smaller treewidth subgraphs is crucial for solving NP-hard problems. While vertex separators with a fixed size can be found efficiently using standard algorithms, finding such subgraphs of small treewidth remains computationally hard. To overcome this barrier, we introduce new techniques and prove that various graph classes—specifically graphs with bounded pathwidth, chordal graphs, interval graphs, chordal bipartite graphs, interval bipartite graphs, and unit disk graphs—possess compact vertex dividers. These structures enable effective problem-solving even when perfect treewidth division is unfeasible. Our main result identifies vertex dividers for these classes with sizes proportional to $(k+O(1))! \cdot 2^{O(k^2)}$, where $k$ represents the target treewidth. By applying these dividers, we achieve faster algorithms for key treewidth-guaranteed NP-hard problems like Clique, Independent Set, and Vertex Cover. Our new methods run in time $2^{O(k^2)} \cdot n$, representing a significant speedup over the best-known previous runtime of $2^{O(k \log k)} n$.

Networks serve as a versatile tool for representing complex, interdependent systems. While foundational concepts like connectedness and clustering are well-understood, recent interest has shifted toward identifying more sophisticated attributes such as communities, groups, and modules. This study clarifies that previously proposed interpretations of such groupings are fundamentally rooted in a "potential" or "association" framework. Specifically, if groups were converted into pairwise relationships, "association" implies symmetry, whereas "potential" implies alignment. The analysis demonstrates that "association" corresponds to unbiased, symmetric, measured relationships, while "potential" relates to biased, alignment-based behaviors that may be inferred or generated. These behaviors typically feature asymmetric, weighted connections characterized by either directional bias toward "in-group" links ("potential") or toward "out-group" links ("association"). By adopting this framework, researchers can distinguish between various modeling approaches for groupings, allowing them to select appropriate methods based on whether their target network exhibits alignment or completion properties. Consequently, this distinction aids in choosing the right weight inference techniques and provides a unified language for diverse network types—including those that are measured, inferred, or derived.

This work presents a new method for identifying Majorana zero-energy states (ZESs) within topological superconductors. The proposed technique involves utilizing a two-layer junction where a non-centrosymmetric superconductor (NCS) connects to an ohmic resistor via a standard NCS electrode. The inclusion of the NCS material is crucial because of its inherent weak superconductivity, which facilitates the emergence of Majorana zero-energy states in the adjacent doped n-type NCS. Simultaneously, the NCS electrode induces bulk tunneling processes, while the attached resistive electrode generates Majorana conductance. The interaction between these two channels allows the scheme to effectively separate ZESs from alternative peaks, such as Andreev bound states. The authors have implemented the current model using numerical calculations based on the Green's function approach, which are further validated against the analytical BTK (Blonder-Tarkin-Serban) framework.

This paper examines the bandit framework with varying action sets, focusing on two distinct objectives: maximizing cumulative regret and maximizing instantaneous reward. While prior research predominantly addresses action sets that are convex, this work analyzes settings that are non-convex. The study evaluates the performance of two specific action sets against an oracle that is assumed to be perfect within the bandit environment. Additionally, the paper explores two real-world applications of varying action sets, including online advertising and social networking, and investigates how this action set flexibility influences model inference. Numerical results indicate that our proposed method outperforms oracle-based benchmarks in terms of cumulative regret and that utilizing smaller action sets can enhance the accuracy of estimated parameters.

A primary challenge in deploying graph neural networks (GNNs) is their heightened vulnerability to adversarial attacks due to the structured nature of graph data. While prior research has largely centered on graph classification tasks, this paper introduces and formalizes the novel problem of data corruption within GNNs for the specific context of graph regression. We investigate scenarios where adversaries introduce contamination into both the labels and target attributes. Our findings reveal that these combined attacks have a significantly larger impact on regression performance than on classification performance. To counteract such attacks, we propose a robust framework utilizing graph reinforcement learning (FRL) designed to identify contaminated nodes. Empirical evidence demonstrates that FRL consistently surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods in accurately locating malicious data. Furthermore, the research explores how attack strategies and the magnitude of attack impacts vary across different graph structures and scenarios.

The automated cross-matching of astronomical catalogs is essential for identifying objects across imaging wavelengths. While astrometry is typically the primary metric for this matching, we propose a new method that augments astrometric metrics with photometric data to improve accuracy. By applying a learnable photometric weight through a neural network, photometric similarities gain increased importance. Consequently, this approach effectively handles contamination caused by astrometrically correct but photometrically mismatched selections, as well as the reverse scenario.

Ontologies serve as standardized formal representations describing domain entities and their interconnections, finding extensive use in diverse fields such as the web, databases, and software engineering. While traditional tools typically offer three-dimensional class diagrams to visualize these complex connections, they often fall short when handling large-scale knowledge graphs. These limitations stem from an inability to accommodate non-hierarchical relations, infinite scrolling requirements that obscure the whole picture, and inadequate support for filtering specific connections. Consequently, this paper introduces OntoPlot, a visualization application engineered to enhance the exploration of massive ontologies. Key innovations include the ability to highlight non-hierarchical relationships, an adaptive navigation system that presents only pertinent filtered information alongside non-filtered data, and a dynamic, user-driven approach to exploring the ontology. Empirical testing using various user studies demonstrates OntoPlot's superior performance in managing non-hierarchical relationships and its efficacy in facilitating the exploration of extensive ontological datasets.

This study introduces a novel framework for improving semi-supervised, end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR). The semi-supervised training process leverages unpaired synthetic speech generated using a Wave-Glow network conditioned on speech text and speaker noise, alongside an auxiliary end-to-end ASR model. This helper model is specifically trained to maximize the cycle-consistency and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) divergence between its recognition outputs on both real and synthetic speech inputs. By enforcing these constraints and combining the models via ensemble methods, the approach ensures that discrepancies in speaker distribution or noise conditions do not degrade synthetic speech performance, thereby enhancing the overall accuracy of the primary semi-supervised ASR system. Empirical results confirm that employing both the synthetic data and the ensemble with the auxiliary model yields significant improvements in Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER) on the clean Librispeech test-clean dataset.

This paper introduces a model-based predictive framework utilizing the concept of active inference, derived from the brain's theory of mind perception. This approach enables robots to make advanced decisions under uncertainty by integrating a perception module with a decision-making process. The active inference decision mechanism employs a specific prediction error to resolve the exploration-exploitation dilemma, eliminating the need for predefined reward functions. Furthermore, a hierarchical process allows robots to achieve complex navigation goals without relying on explicit motion models. The efficacy of this approach was validated through simulations and real-world experiments involving 2D navigation and obstacle avoidance. The results demonstrate that after just a few trials, a 2D robot can successfully navigate to a designated target using a perception and action system that requires no prior knowledge of motion parameters. Moreover, a hierarchical implementation enables autonomous robotics to accomplish intricate navigation goals within a 2D environment without any motion model initialization, learning the necessary dynamics entirely through trial-and-error interactions.

This research investigates the contribution of soft features inherent to molecules and their capacity for local deformation and freedom of motion to the Soret effect. Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that a soft Lennard-Jones Solute-Solvent system exhibits stronger thermophoretic migration than a hard counterpart, revealing that internal degrees of freedom significantly enhance the migration mechanism. This significant influence is further substantiated by theoretical calculations of thermophoretic drift and comparisons with molecular diffusion. This evidence underscores the critical role of soft characteristics in molecular transport phenomena under temperature gradients.

Comprehensive evaluation of computer-generated grammar compositions is vital for boosting the proficiency of machine writing systems within composition domains. Previous research has primarily focused on developing domain-specific cut-off metrics. Conversely, this study introduces a more effective domain-agnostic approach that leverages the fine-tuning of pre-trained transformer-based language models. We conducted a comparative analysis of various available transformer architectures and determined that a BERT model performs best for evaluation tasks when applied to a dataset of 1,500 samples. We further refined the model's precision using a dataset of 500 samples. Finally, we applied a human-in-the-loop mechanism to filter out low confidence predictions. We found that this automated method surpassed the performance of current state-of-the-art evaluation metrics.

Adapting pedestrian identification models to hit the best possible accuracy rate is a challenge, but the reason false positives happen is still not entirely clear. In this paper, we introduce an unsupervised false positive reduction method called Box Re-Ranking. Our approach is based on the idea that the model's confidence score box is not always reliable. In order to improve accuracy rate, we use a simple two stage filter that is based on motion information and image quality control. Our test results are very good and show that the method is able to reduce false positives by 30% on the well known PedDet2018 test set.

We introduce a neural framework designed to transform poor-quality audio signals into high-fidelity stereo recordings. The system initially processes stereo channels independently by mapping one-dimensional (1D) temporal data into two-dimensional (2D) spatio-temporal representations, effectively functioning as a 2D image-based neural audio model. Subsequently, it converts this derived image into a high-quality stereo audio signal. Experimental results indicate that this approach outperforms current state-of-the-art models in the domain.

This study introduces FauxThrow, a novel tool designed to simulate inaccurate release points during ball throwing tasks. Throwing constitutes a critical action in numerous settings, including sports, military operations, and military simulations, yet existing benchmarks predominantly depend on human execution, which is costly and unsafe when deploying balls at high velocities. To address these limitations, we developed an advanced robot arm capable of generating diverse throwing trajectories while using a vision system to pinpoint the exact point of release through ball occlusion analysis. Our system was tested by performing repeated, both standard and faulty throws, analyzing the resulting variations in ball trajectory, release velocity, and release angle through statistical examination. Our findings reveal a direct dependency between the release point and all three throw parameters; specifically, moving the release location even by a few millimeters can drastically alter the ball's path, speed, and trajectory. Consequently, this research confirms the necessity for precise points of release to achieve consistent throws and lays the groundwork for future throwing systems.

Neural machine translation (NMT) frameworks typically rely on sequential models to generate translations in an order from left to right. Consequently, they often fail to produce outputs that strictly align with syntactic tree structures, even when these translations concur correctly. To resolve this issue, we introduce a top-down, syntax-guided approach to machine translation that permits the generation of tree constructions alongside syntactic links—edges arising from leaves that should directly connect, albeit at lower probabilities. This methodology utilizes a single-topple decoder capable of branching to select a child node or a link at any step. By leveraging our proposed "one-pass" model, we achieve a significantly faster generation speed compared to current two-pass systems used in translation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model can learn effective priorities for producing specific sub-trees or links during a left-to right one-pass mode. Even within this sequential phase, we observe a marked improvement in translation fluency and accuracy when the model successfully predicts a higher density of essential links versus neglecting them.

Accurate knowledge of reaction rates is essential for deciphering both the astrochemical dynamics of the interstellar medium and the formation processes of prebiotic molecules within protoplanetary disks. A critical component in determining these rates is knowing the binding energy, $D_0$, which describes how a gas-phase species adheres to a grain surface. This information is vital for calculating reaction probabilities against thermal desorption and understanding whether a reaction occurs while a species is physisorbed. However, existing quantum chemical predictions for $D_0$ are often inconsistent due to a lack of a unified computational protocol and standard reference data. To resolve this, we have developed the Binding Energy Assessment (BEE) platform, a system that systematically evaluates $D_0$ values using a single shared protocol. To begin populating this database, we utilized quantum chemical calculations to determine the binding energies for 115 hydrogen-containing molecules interacting with water, amorphous carbon, and amorphous silicate surfaces. Our findings indicate that current estimates for a single reaction case can diverge by as much as a factor of 2.5. Consequently, this study represents the initial substantial contribution to the BEE public database.

This work examines a heterogeneous stochastic multiplicative process where a walk's minimum limit is contingent upon its sample count. While standard multiplicative processes are well-understood, this specific process exhibits atypical characteristics; it initially resembles a random walk with geometric drift before transitioning into a process of uniform diffusion. We present an analytical approach to its probability density function and contrast the theoretical predictions with simulation outcomes to validate our analysis. Furthermore, we explore the theoretical framework in a context analogous to financial markets, utilizing a minimum limit analogous to investors' loss aversion. Both the statistical behavior of such markets and their dynamic evolution from a drift-dominated phase to a diffusion phase mirror one another. This approach offers a mathematical explanation for why financial assets frequently exhibit geometric behavior initially before eventually becoming dominated by diffusion.

We introduce **Shallow Shades**, a randomized medium-depth quantum circuit designed to evaluate human expectations of specific phenomena. This approach is highly adaptable to various topics and can be executed using only a small number (10-20) of qubits. Our findings from an experiment involving 100 participants exploring general expectations of causality reveal a categorical split: participants' quantum response distributions for scenarios with positive causality are distinctly separate from those with negative causality, mirroring human behavioral patterns. However, these findings hold true only for immediate (direct) causal links; in indirect cases, participant expectations overlap and are not statistically discernible. Crucially, Shallow Shades successfully captures the nuances of human causality data, distinguishing clearly between direct causal relationships and overlapping predictions for indirect ones.

This work addresses the scattering initialization for the initial-value problem associated with the non-integrable second-generation (DS-II) equations. A significant finding is that the initial data's $L^2$ norm exhibits substantial local concentration across a broad spectrum of the spectral parameter $|k|$. This distribution deviates markedly from the conventional expectation of global concentration at high $|k|$. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the reflection coefficient's dependence on $|k|$ is non-negligible. These findings collectively indicate that the reflection coefficient cannot be approximated as being concentrated solely in the high $|k|$ regime.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models are surprisingly sensitive to minor alterations, such as arithmetic errors in weight parameters or slight modifications to the vocabulary. This fragility is particularly problematic for low-resource Machine Translation, where limited data necessitates lightweight and efficient models. Addressing this, we introduce a novel approach to creating such models. Our study evaluates extraction techniques that produce smaller architectures by comparing them against post-quantization methods, which yield lighter models without sacrificing performance. Our findings indicate that, unlike post-quantization models, successfully extracted lightweight versions are more resilient to disturbances. This robustness is especially evident in low-data scenarios, making the extraction approach promising for developing reliable low-resource translation systems.

Deep learning approaches for medical image segmentation typically necessitate vast amounts of labeled data. To mitigate this requirement, researchers have developed strategies such as transfer learning, domain adaptation, and data augmentation. This paper introduces a method leveraging supplementary data from external sources to enhance model performance in low-label environments. We demonstrate that combining self-supervised learning with unsupervised clustering effectively yields superior segmentation results for pneumonia compared to supervised-only baselines. Additionally, unsupervised clustering facilitates the generation of robust feature embeddings that can serve as input for supervised or fully unsupervised clustering-based segmentation frameworks. Comprehensive experiments were conducted on two datasets: a private repository of chest X-rays labeled for pneumonia and the public CheXpert dataset containing 150,000 labeled images. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/pneumonia_segmentation_clustering.

Image captioning models are often over-associating visual objects with frequent word choices, which can result in unexpectedly biased outputs. We present a solution that utilizes open-book transformer models and regulate these biases through pre-training adjustments using auxiliary labels. This method effectively compels the model to generate word choices proportional to the input distribution, which is calculated by removing top-frequent terms from the vocabulary. This approach is implemented via an optimal auxiliary loss function designed for this purpose. We demonstrate that including this auxiliary loss does not have any negative impact on the quality or the generation of these captions. This method is particularly effective in suppressing a wide range of these word biases. This approach is further demonstrated by analyzing these captions and highlight specific words that are avoided, which reveals a more in-depth understanding of the nature of these word biases within the model's outputs. This study also includes a human-based evaluation to assess the effectiveness of this method in these areas. This research is based on the work presented in the paper, which is available at the following link: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-06135-3_35.

We present an expanded definition of the damage metric for causal structures, applicable to generalized metrics such as causal distances. While this extension aligns closely with intuitive expectations in simple scenarios, several examples demonstrate that the damage metric exhibits surprising properties and behaves counterintuitively in complex scenarios.

Deep learning techniques are increasingly being adopted across a broad spectrum of industries and scientific disciplines due to their exceptional predictive capabilities. However, traditional commercial APIs for deep learning are often rigid, restricting users to pre-defined models and fixed batch sizes. In response to these limitations, we introduce MMLSpark, a robust and scalable deep learning framework designed to seamlessly integrate with Apache Spark. This framework offers an intuitive, user-driven API capable of orchestrating complex deep learning architectures, thereby delivering heightened flexibility alongside extended development timelines and shorter training durations.

Text-to-Speech (TTS) technology converts written text into audible speech. While it is a fundamental technology with extensive applications, the proliferation of new languages and dialects has outpaced current capabilities, rendering it difficult to create audio for these lesser-known linguistic variants. This paper introduces a zero-shot approach to TTS, enabling the system to generate speech for dialects and languages without requiring specific training data. This is achieved by training a neural network to extract and combine language and dialect embeddings, a process enhanced by incorporating textual and acoustic contextual cues. The resulting model has been evaluated on three language/dialect pairs and demonstrates the potential to significantly broaden the text-to audio scope to encompass speech for communities currently excluded by traditional methods.

This study examines a thermal model described by a thermal equation incorporating a nonlinear heat relaxation term, where the dynamic boundary conditions represent constraints for contact with thermal relaxation. The research focuses on demonstrating the existence and single-valued nature of this system's solution. The demonstration relies on generating an approximate solution through discrete time schemes and then deriving the solution as a byproduct of the convergence of these schemes, which was established using the weakly compact, accretive, and surjective operator of a linear $m$-monotone graph.

The increasing adoption of renewable energy sources, driven by their lower costs and higher efficiency, has necessitated the integration of distributed photovoltaic (PV) systems into the smart grid. To support grid operators and enable the wider adoption of these technologies, accurate forecasting of their impact is essential. This paper introduces a methodology for predicting the daily peak load in low-voltage distribution areas, which involves combining one-dimensional and two-dimensional LSTM models. Model performance was evaluated using datasets from Germany and the United Kingdom, demonstrating that the proposed fusion approach achieves superior accuracy compared to existing methods.

We introduce a structured framework for synthesizing domain expertise throughout the machine learning lifecycle, spanning development to operations. Rooted in the DevOps paradigm and tailored specifically for data science, it forms the basis of "Machine Learning Domain Expertise Integration" (MLEI). Our objective is to empower practitioners with diverse backgrounds—whether data scientists, domain experts, or operations staff—to collaboratively manage specialized knowledge regarding data, infrastructure, and workflows. To achieve this, we have developed a cross-functional tool called the "Knowledge Matrix," designed to facilitate the systematic organization of domain expert insights within the broader ML workflow.

The ongoing spread of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) has precipitated a global pandemic, characterized by a lack of a cure or vaccine. Since respiratory difficulties are a primary symptom, doctors are increasingly relying on Computerized Tomography (CT) scans to evaluate lung function and detect the virus early. While automated diagnosis through CT imaging could expedite treatment and curb transmission, existing deep learning models for this task are often biased by the statistical distribution of training data, which hinders their real-world applicability. This study introduces the Weakly Guided Lesion Localization (WGL) algorithm, a framework designed to perform unbiased training on CT scans for identifying COVID-19 abnormalities. The method utilizes a two-stage process: a teacher network first estimates the organ of origin for each slice, while a student learning to mimic the teacher but is regularized to align its predictions with the teacher's information gain. Experiments on two distinct datasets demonstrate that while our method matches the accuracy of advanced techniques, it outperforms them specifically in regions far from lesions as well as in terms of model convergence.

Recognizing and localizing vertebrae is essential for diagnosing spinal diseases. Although established deep learning frameworks have improved vertebral segmentation and classification, they often neglect anatomical consistency and suffer from inaccurate localization due to skewed training data. This study introduces a new deep learning strategy to rectify spines in CT images, thereby enhancing the localization and recognition of vertebrae. We address the recognition challenge through an anatomically grounded neural network that models vertebral structures, thereby promoting intervertebral correlation and spatial coherence. Furthermore, the proposed localization technique incorporates constraints derived from this recognition module. Experimental outcomes indicate that these methods substantially enhance the training efficiency of the localization system while boosting inference accuracy.

We present an initial theoretical model of "cavity-stabilized scattering," in which the resonant interaction between photons and excitons or electrons within an optical resonator is influenced by strong light-coupling dynamics. This work extends the scattering formalism to the non-perturbative ultrastrong-coupling (USC) regime and demonstrates that the resulting antiresonant scattering can lead to the dynamical stabilization of an excitonic or cavitionic state against environmental decoherence. Specifically, we analyze resonant scattering by electron waves, revealing that the dynamical stabilization of the cavity polariton state arises from the antiresonant behavior of the electron wave, whose motion is non-perturbatively governed by light-matter interactions in the USC limit. More concretely, resonant electron involvement generates standing electron waves characterized by Fabry-Perot-type features, whose positions rely on cavity resonance; conversely, non-resonant electron involvement produces traveling standing waves lacking such constraints. Consequently, non-resonant electron waves exhibit dispersion akin to bare electrons uncoupled from light, whereas resonant ones adhere to resonant electron involvement characteristics. Moreover, the model predicts a robust cavity-stabilized state persisting even when light-coupling interactions surpass the bare electron transition energy. While electric actuators are standard in modern quadruped robots, they are being increasingly targeted for robotic research due to their high cost and limited runtime. In contrast, pneumatic actuators offer a compelling alternative with superior power density, high loading capabilities, rapid response times, high packing density, and significant energy efficiency. However, the elasticity inherent to these pneumatic systems complicates control strategies. This paper introduces a new control methodology designed to leverage, rather than compensate for, actuator compliance. By employing reinforcement learning to discover locomotion strategies that fully harness structural flexibility, we demonstrate enhanced walking capabilities on both flat and uneven surfaces alongside improved dynamic performance. Furthermore, our approach inherently adapts movement patterns to real-time environmental feedback. Validation across multiple PC-based dry-run simulations alongside tests on a physically instantiated quadruped confirms the efficacy of this compliant-based control scheme.

This work introduces a novel framework aimed at mitigating the issue of quantum distinguishability. By introducing a new functional for distinguishing quantum states, the authors extend quantum information theory to include symmetric non-commuting operators as their foundational elements. Through the construction of specific matrices and the application of the H\"{o}lder and Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities, a new metric is derived to quantify the distinguishability between any two such operators. The study demonstrates that this new functional exhibits the requisite properties of a valid metric.

This work introduces and investigates a magnetic tearing mechanism within slab plasmas that operates at a micro-scale, distinct from the conventional mechanism based on a resistivity-derived diffusion region. In our proposed system, the process is governed by a non-resistive, collisionless relaxation of the anisotropic pressure tensor, resulting in the formation of a significantly smaller diffusion region. This non-resistive nature suggests that the effect could potentially drive magnetic reconnection in the collisionless environments of space. Our analysis indicates that the scale of this region is dictated by the anisotropy of the pressure tensor and the characteristic time of its relaxation. Utilizing particle-in-cell simulations, we demonstrate that the mechanism is consistent with the relativistic and collisionless plasma conditions found in the magnetotail of the Earth's space environment. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the effect is robust and can be triggered by a broad spectrum of plasma parameters.

Current fashion-specific trait manipulation research is largely confined to color and pattern alterations, which proves insufficient for next-generation fashion retrieval systems. The desired future systems necessitate the ability to modify diverse traits—such as altering a garment's color, changing a model's hair style, or adjusting their hair type—and subsequently matching these edited images with appropriate database descriptions. To address this gap, we introduce "Semi-supervised Feature-Level Trait Manipulation for Fashion Image Retrieval" (S-FL-TM), a comprehensive, end-to-end framework. Our approach first extracts specific traits from source images, then utilizes two sub-models to generate corresponding edited versions. Subtly, a retrieval engine is employed to locate appropriate modification instances, while supertly, a classification model ensures the integrity of manipulated features. Notably, this study is the inaugural to synthesize both fine-grained detection and high-quality editing capabilities for fashion-specific modifications. Furthermore, we have assembled a novel, large-scale dataset, "In-Store," containing 100,000 images of over 500 in-store shoppers, each exhibiting distinct traits. Extensive experiments validate the system's efficacy, marking a significant leap forward in state-of-the-art fashion image retrieval technologies.

We introduce a framework for addressing an extensive range of linear ill-posed issues within the broad context of Banach spaces. At the core of our methodology is a dual formulation, which enables the integration of prior information as constraints in a dual frame rather than as regularizer penalties. This approach yields two primary advantages: first, it circumvents the lack of convexity often found in the associated original problems; second, it enhances numerical tractability by reducing the original equation, regardless of its dimensionality, to a lower-dimensional dual system. We demonstrate the utility of this methodology regarding $L^p$ spaces ($1 < p < \infty$) and the resolution of inverse problems. Furthermore, the paper provides a convergence analysis for a newly developed dual gradient descent algorithm applied to the resulting $L^p$-space formulations derived from this method.

We introduce a novel dataset featuring both color and multi-view perspectives, along with annotated 3D models in voxel format. The collection comprises over 100 objects captured under more than 300 diverse lighting conditions to support training a view synthesis neural network. To ensure robust handling of occluded regions during reconstruction, our approach employs a dynamic occlusion mask and a specialized loss function designed to enhance depth estimation accuracy in these areas while minimizing errors caused by filled-in regions surrounding occlusions. Extensive testing on this dataset confirms that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, delivering superior performance in reconstructing occluded areas and estimating depth within such complex regions.

In multi-hop IEEE 802.11 networks, both the choice of access points (APs)/extenders and their placement significantly impact performance. This paper introduces a method for selecting appropriate AP/extendors based on channel load in domestic wireless environments utilizing IEEE 802.11k/v. Implemented in a practical 802.11n/20211ac architecture, the approach involves utilizing fast query responses to gather active AP/extendor data, assessing local channel load across all 11 channels per radio frequency, and directing clients to the optimal AP/extendor positioned on this least congested frequency. Furthermore, the mechanism facilitates an optimal number of extensors, which mitigates signal retransmission issues caused by overlapping signals and channel congestion. Performance is validated through extensive experiments in a residential setting. The system is built upon the open source hostapd client and a custom Python implementation of 802.11k/v protocols. The source code is available at https://github.com/andrewbelyan/ch_load_ap_select.
